KEY MESSAGE 1...A frontal system passes through the region 
later today and tonight producing widespread showers with 
localized flash flooding.

A mid level short wave trough will continue to progress 
eastward through tonight. A warm front ahead of that low, was 
over central PA and central NJ as of mid day. That front is 
expected to progress eastward into our region late this evening
into the overnight hours.

The focus is on a convective complex that developed over Ohio
earlier this afternoon and is making progress eastward across
central PA and MD at this hour. Most hi-res guidance continues
to show this complex at least clipping portions of our region,
mainly across the southern half of our forecast area. As of now,
current time of arrival, depicts possibly around the 9 PM
timeframe at the earliest. However, by this point, instability 
will be more limited and continue to wane, so it appears likely
that this complex will continue to weaken as it approaches. 
That being said, we will continue to monitor for the heavy rain 
and damaging wind threats.

With very high PWATs, localized flash flooding is possible due 
to localized amounts of 1 to 2 inches of rain, despite the 
convective complex moving through rather quickly. The Weather 
Prediction Center has a Marginal Risk for Excessive Rainfall, 
which is a 1 out of 4. The Slight risk has been cut back to 
portions to southeast Pennsylvania west of Philadelphia.

The severe threat is fairly minimal, generally focused on
Delmarva where the Storm Prediction Center has a Marginal Risk
(1 out of 5) for Delmarva and extreme southern New Jersey.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A trailing mid-level short wave trough and weak
cold front lead to the potential for additional rounds of 
showers and thunderstorms on Monday.

The cold front associated with the low that approaches the 
region on Sunday will finally progress through the region and 
move offshore on Monday. Additionally, in the the mid-levels, a 
trailing short wave trough will cross overhead. The net result 
is that isolated to scattered showers and thunderstorms will be 
possible primarily during the afternoon on Monday. 

As for hazards, this round appears to have very limited threats
for both flash flooding and severe weather. Convection on 
Monday will be much more weakly forced (as compared to 
Sunday/Sunday night), and bulk shear values are depicted in the 
20 to 25 kt range, which is rather modest. Although there will 
be instability present, the modest shear will limit storm 
organization. Model soundings still depict relatively high 
precipitable water values of upwards of 2 inches, and warm cloud
layers above 10K ft, which results in some heavy rain threat. 
However, with limited shear and coverage of convection, the 
threat for any one area to get heavy rain for long enough to 
result in flash flooding remains low.

For those hoping for a significant cool down in the wake of 
this cold front, unfortunately the temperature gradient is very 
small. As such highs on Tuesday will be at or just a degree or 
two lower than Monday. That being said, the front should usher 
in drier air, so regardless it should feel more comfortable on 
Tuesday. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...A cold front is expected to cross through the 
region Wednesday night into Thursday resulting in more shower 
and thunderstorm chances.

In the wake of Monday night's cold front, weak high pressure 
will briefly build into the region for Tuesday and much of 
Wednesday. An upper-low will traverse portions of Ontario and 
Quebec during this time, passing north of the region Wednesday 
night. To the south of the upper-low, broad troughing will be in
place across much of the Northeast, with a few embedded 
shortwaves pivoting around the base of the trough. At the 
surface, a cold front will begin to approach the area late 
Wednesday, and cross through the region Wednesday night into 
Thursday. 

Timing discrepancies remain with the frontal passage amongst 
model guidance. Some guidance indicates the front passing 
through the region primarily during the overnight hours 
Wednesday night and clearing the region Thursday morning, while 
there is still some guidance to suggest slower timing. At this 
point, timing uncertainties limit confidence in whether or not 
there will be any notable severe weather or flash flooding 
concerns, but this will continue to bear watching, particularly 
if the slower solutions come to fruition. For now, PoPs peak in 
the 40-60% range across most of the area on Thursday. 

There are also some indications that the pattern may remain 
unsettled into the weekend as the front could get hung up just 
south of the region with a couple of areas of low pressure 
riding along it and mid-level troughing remaining in place. PoPs
are currently in the 20-40% range each day due to the present 
uncertainties in timing and placement of these features.
